sections.heading: The Seven Holy Youths of Ephesus

pairs.en: On the same day, the fourth of the month, we remember the holy SEVEN YOUTHS of Ephesus: MAXIMILIAN, EXACUSTODIANUS, IAMBLICHUS, MARTINIAN, DIONYSIUS, ANTONINUS and CONSTANTINE.
*I honour the sevenfold choir of martyrs,* *who showed the world the rising of the dead.* *On the fourth the seven, raised from the dead, died together.*

These saints lived in the reign of the emperor Decius, in the year 252. They gave away everything they had to the poor, went into a cave and hid there; and they begged God to release them from the bonds of the body rather than let them be handed over to the emperor Decius — and so they gave up their souls to God. When the emperor Decius came back to Ephesus, he sent for them to come and sacrifice to the idols; and learning that they had died inside the cave, he ordered the mouth of the cave to be walled up.

From that time, three hundred and seventy-two years passed, until the thirty-eighth year of the reign of Theodosius the Younger — that is, the year 446. At that time a heresy sprang up that said there is no resurrection of the dead. The emperor Theodosius saw the Church of God thrown into confusion, because many bishops had been led astray by this heresy, and he did not know what to do. So he put on a garment of hair, spread himself out on the ground and wept, begging God to show him the way out of this heresy.

The Lord did not overlook his tears; he heard him in the following way. The owner of the hill where the cave of the seven holy youths lay wanted, just at that time, to build a fold for his flock. And as he was rolling stones away from the cave to build the fold, the door of the cave was opened — and by the command of God, the seven youths who had died in the cave rose up and began talking with one another, as if they had only gone to sleep the night before. They were entirely unchanged — even their clothes had not decayed at all in the natural damp and moisture of the cave.

When they got up, they had it in mind that the emperor Decius was still looking for them, to torture them, and they talked it over among themselves. Maximilian said to the others: “Brothers, if we are arrested by Decius, let us stand bravely, and not betray the nobility of our faith. And you, brother Iamblichus, go and buy bread — but buy more this time, because yesterday evening you bought little, and that is why we went to sleep hungry. And find out what Decius is deciding about us.”

So Iamblichus went into the city of Ephesus, and he saw the sign of the precious Cross on the gate, and he was amazed. Then he saw it in other places too, and noticing the houses changed and the people different, he thought he was seeing a vision, or that he had gone out of his mind. He went on to the bakers, took the bread, and when he handed them the coins he hurried to get back to the cave. But he noticed the bakers passing the coins from one to another and looking at him, saying that he had found a treasure — because the coin he had given them bore plain witness that he had found a treasure: it had stamped on it the image of an emperor who had reigned many years before.

When Iamblichus heard this he trembled, and from fear he could not speak, thinking that he had been recognised and would be handed over by them to the emperor Decius. So he begged them, saying: “Please, my masters, keep my money, take your bread as well, and let me go.” But the bakers said: “Show us the treasure you found, and make us partners in the find — and if not, we will hand you over to death.” And seeing that the holy man stood there lost in thought, they put a chain around his neck and dragged him into the market.

They brought him before the proconsul of Ephesus and stood him up for questioning. The proconsul looked at him and said: “Tell me, young man, how did you find the treasure, and how big is it, and where?” Iamblichus answered that he had never found any treasure — the coin he had given them he had from his parents. “And what this thing is that has happened to me,” he said, “I do not know.”

The proconsul asked him again: “What city are you from?” The saint answered: “I am from this city — if this city is Ephesus.” And the proconsul: “Who are your parents? Let them come to us, and when the truth comes to light, then we will believe you.” Iamblichus answered: “Such-and-such is my father, such-and-such is my grandfather, and such-and-such is my kinsman.” And the proconsul said to him: “The names you have given are foreign and unheard of, nothing like the names in use today — so you cannot be believed on their strength.” Iamblichus said: “If you will not believe me when I tell the truth, I have nothing more to say.” The proconsul answered: “You godless man, your coin testifies by its inscription that it was struck three hundred years ago and more, in the days of the emperor Decius — and you, a young man, are trying to cheat us?”

Then Iamblichus fell at the feet of those present and begged them: “Please, my masters, tell me — where is the emperor Decius, who was in this city?” They told him: “Decius is not among the living in these times; he died many years ago.” And Iamblichus said: “Is that why you are astonished, my masters? Then come with me, let us go to the cave, and from the proofs themselves my words will be believed. For I know that we fled because of Decius — and that yesterday, when I went to buy bread, I saw that Decius had entered this city.”

That is what the saint said. The bishop of Ephesus, whose name was Marinus, heard it and said to the proconsul: “I think something wonderful has happened in this affair — so let us go with him.” So the proconsul and the bishop and many others followed him. When they reached the cave, Iamblichus went in first, and then the bishop — who, turning to the right-hand side of the cave's door, saw a casket sealed with two seals, which the Christians Rufinus and Theodore had placed there. Those were the men who had been sent by Decius with others to wall up the door of the cave, and they are the ones who also wrote the record of these saints and inscribed their names on tablets of lead.

So when all the leading men had gathered together with the proconsul, they opened the casket and found the lead tablets inside; and when they read what was written on them, they were all beside themselves. Going on into the inner part of the cave, they found the saints, and fell at their feet; then they sat down and questioned them. The saints told them first their own story, and then the crimes of the emperor Decius — and everyone was amazed, and glorified the God of wonders.

Then the proconsul and the bishop wrote a report to the emperor Theodosius and announced all these things to him. When the emperor read the letter he was filled with joy at such news, and went in great haste to Ephesus. Entering the cave, he fell to the ground and washed the feet of the saints with his tears; and his soul rejoiced and was glad, because the Lord had not overlooked his prayer, but had shown him, with his own eyes, the resurrection of the dead. And while the emperor was talking with the saints, with the bishops and many other rulers present, the saints dozed a little — and so, in front of them all, they gave their souls into the hands of God.

Then the emperor gave costly robes and plenty of gold and silver, and ordered seven caskets to be made, so that the relics of the saints could be laid in them. But that very night the saints appeared to the emperor and said: “Leave us, your majesty, in this cave, in which we were raised.” So a great assembly of bishops and rulers was held, and the emperor laid the relics of the saints in the ground of the cave, just as they had shown him in the vision. He made a joyful feast, entertained the poor of Ephesus with great hospitality, and gladdened all the people, honouring them lavishly and royally. He also released from prison the bishops who had been imprisoned for preaching the resurrection of the dead. And so it became a common feast for everyone, glorifying and blessing our Lord Jesus Christ. (Note that the Greek life of these saints survives in the Great Lavra on Mount Athos; it begins: “The Master and Maker of all things.”)

sections.heading: Saint Eudocia, and the bringing of her relics

pairs.en: On the same day we remember our holy mother and martyr EUDOCIA, and the bringing of her relics.
*What fragrance is this?* *The body of Eudocia* *comes breathing out the graces of her contest.*

This holy martyr of Christ, Eudocia, came from the East. She was taken prisoner by the Persians and carried off to Persia, and because she was well taught in the holy Scriptures, she taught all the other captives. So she became known to the Persian women and beloved by them, and she turned many of them to the knowledge of God. For this she was denounced to the judges and flogged with ox-hide whips; then she was thrown into prison, and she stayed there two months.

After that she was tried again, and because she confessed Christ as the true God, she was beaten so hard with thorny rods of the pomegranate tree that her flesh came apart and fell to the ground, and the men beating her were spattered red with her blood. Then they threw her back into prison. When six months had passed, they brought her out and tried her a third time. They split reeds to the measure of her body, stripped her, and swaddled her naked in the reeds all around; then they pulled the reeds tight with a thin cord — so tight that the reeds bit into the flesh of her body. After that they dragged each reed away by force, and with it they dragged and tore her flesh. That is how those inhuman men brought the martyr the sharpest and most unbearable pain.

Then they hanged the saint, and binding her whole body tightly with ropes they crushed all her bones. When they saw that she was half dead and could no longer speak, they cut off her holy head — and so this manly-souled woman went to heaven wearing her crown. Later her holy relic was brought back, welling up healings for those who run to it with faith.
The holy martyr THATHOUEL died by hanging from an apple tree.
*Hanged on an apple tree, Thathouel, you die —* *to pick for yourself the strange fruit of Eden.*

sections.heading: The dedication of the church of the Pantokrator

pairs.en: On the same day, the anniversary of the dedication of the beautiful and holy church of the imperial monastery of our Lord and God and Saviour Jesus Christ the Pantokrator, in Constantinople.

sections.heading: Saint Kosmas of Aetolia, the new priest-martyr

pairs.en: The holy new priest-martyr and equal-to-the-apostles KOSMAS, who suffered in Albania in the year 1779, died by strangling.
*Blessed Kosmas — you proved a true “kosmos,” an adornment;* *you graced the world with your words, and with your blood.*
Through the prayers of your Saints, Christ our God, have mercy on us.
In some copies, John is written instead of Antoninus.

By the chronology of Meletios of Athens, the sleep of the seven holy youths does not come to three hundred and seventy-two years, but only to a hundred and ninety-eight: take the two hundred and fifty-two years, in which they fell asleep, from the four hundred and forty-six, in which they rose, and a hundred and ninety-eight remain.

*The text goes wrong here: the figure should be 194, not 198.* *Note also that these saints must have fallen asleep before the year 252, since Decius was no longer alive then.* *See also 22 October.* — the 1868 editor
The commemoration and the life of the holy martyr Ia are written here in the Menaia to no purpose, because they were already written on the eleventh of September.
In the manuscript Synaxarist, a set of iambic verses on the Monastery of the Pantokrator is written at this point; it has been left out, as worthless.
For the martyrdom of Saint Kosmas, see the New Martyrologion.
